newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FEATURE - Malaysia plans world's longest building.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Malaysia plans world's longest building.

text.p: Malaysia, home to the world's tallest twin buildings, has launched an ambitious plan to construct its longest.
A 2.4 km (1.4-mile) long building called GigaWorld will be part of a five to 10 billion ringgit ($2.5 to $4 billion) commercial riverside project called KL LinearCity.
Its developers say GigaWorld will overtake the current world's longest building -- a 1.0 km (0.60 mile) shopping mall in Edmonton, Canada -- and help turn the Malaysian capital into a "global city".
David Chew, managing director of developers KL LinearCity Sdn Bhd said GigaWorld had been given its name because it was bigger than "mega" projects seen around the world.
"We feel that the development of GigaWorld justifies something that is beyond all these mega projects. The next descriptor after mega is giga," Chew told Reuters in an interview.
Kuala Lumpur, popularly known as KL for short, already has the world's tallest buildings, the Petronas Twin Towers, each 88 storeys and 452 metres (1,482 feet) high.
The twin buildings surpassed the previous record holder, the Sears Tower in Chicago, by 10 metres (33 feet).
KL also has Southeast Asia's tallest telecommunications tower, the 421-metre (1,380-foot) Kuala Lumpur Tower.
KL LinearCity developers say the 10-storey tube-like GigaWorld will be built on stilts over the Klang river, which snakes through the city centre.
The complex will have theme parks, shopping malls, offices, hotels, condominiums and parking areas for 10,000 cars.
It will also have an artificial river for leisure boating on the seventh floor. A travelator will move visitors quickly from one end of the complex to the other.
The entire project is to be built in stages over the next 20 to 25 years, with the first phase expected to be completed in 1999.
To ease access, its developers will build a 2.2 billion ringgit elevated monorail system called People-mover Rapid Transit (PRT) alongside the building.
The project aims to clean up the murky river and green the riverbank with parks, as well as facilitate new property development, said Chew.
Development agreements have been signed between KL LinearCity, the Malaysia government, a state property firm and the Kuala Lumpur City Council.
Under the agreements, the developers have been given a 99-year lease on 216.5 acres (88 hectares) of government-owned river land for 611 million ringgit.
Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, a strong backer of the project, witnessed the signing ceremony.
Though critics have described the project as grandiose, Mahathir said it would be a new, unique feature of the Kuala Lumpur skyline.
Asked by reporters if Kuala Lumpur needed to build the world's longest building, Mahathir retorted: "Why not? Is there any reason why it doesn't need (to)?"
Developer Chew said KL LinearCity, along with Petronas Twin Towers, Kuala Lumpur Tower and a planned new $3.6 billion airport would put the capital city on the world map.
"The idea of LinearCity was a unique opportunity to help in the quantum leap...to put Kuala Lumpur into the league of global cities," he said.
Answering charges that the project would further pollute the Klang river, Chew said the opposite would happen.
"Today the river is in a poor state. It's difficult to make it worse by our development," he said.

The developers' plan to resettle about 1,000 families who live along the river and are a cause of the pollution, he said. There are also plans to clean and deepen the river as well as starting flood-mitigation schemes, he said.
KL LinearCity Sdn Bhd is led by chairman Kamarudin Jaffar, an advisor to Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim.

His board of directors includes tycoon Vincent Tan, chief executive officer of diversified Berjaya Group Bhd, and Wan Adli Wan Ibrahim, executive chairman of Transwater Corp Bhd, which through a subsidiary has a privatisation contract to run Malaysia's sewerage treatment systems.
KL LinearCity Sdn Bhd has paid-up capital of 50 million ringgit and authorised capital of 300 million ringgit.
The project is expected to be financed by a mix of shareholders' equity and commercial debt financing, Chew said.
The company is preparing to secure a listing on the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange under new rules introduced last year allowing new infrastructure projects to be publicly traded. ($1=2.5 ringgit)
